items.title: A Voice Bigger Than One State
items.alt: Charlee Cromwell at the Pentagon briefing podium in Washington, D.C.
items.hook: An Iowa teen carries the voices of National Guard youth into national conversations.
items.quote: No matter how small you are or what state you are from, your voice can be heard. People want to hear you.
body: During two national youth leadership trips, Charlee and other military-connected youth worked together on issues affecting families across the country. At both events, they met directly with military officials to discuss concerns that reached beyond the National Guard and reflected experiences across the military community.

Throughout those conversations, Charlee kept the Guard Teen Panel goal in focus: improve the experiences of military-connected youth and empower them to speak up in their communities, states, regions, and country.
The experience helped shape the leader she is becoming. It showed her that making a difference matters deeply to her, and that a young person's voice can carry far beyond a hometown or home state.
items.impact: Whether all twelve GTP members were together or only three National Guard youth were in the room, their purpose stayed the same: advocate for the 53,600 National Guard teens across the states, territories, and the District of Columbia.

items.title: An Evening That Strengthened the Bonds Behind the Uniform
items.alt: Families gathered together at the Military Family Ball
items.hook: An evening of belonging gave military families room to connect, breathe, and build resilience together.
items.quote: They provide valuable opportunities for our family to connect with other military families, fostering community, shared understanding, and mutual support.
body: As Month of the Military Child came to a close, Iowa CYP brought families together for an evening that went far beyond a traditional event. The Military Family Ball created space for connection, understanding, and shared experience.
Youth connected quickly, parents found people who understood the rhythm of military life, and families built relationships that could continue after the evening ended.
Those moments strengthen resilience in youth, reinforce family relationships, and create support networks that matter during deployment and transition.
items.impact: Community partners and 22 volunteers helped deliver a 10-out-of-10 experience, with nearly half of participating families attending an Iowa CYP event for the first time.

gallery.alt: Families connecting at the Military Family Ball

items.title: Iowa Launches Purple Star Schools
items.alt: Students, families, school leaders, and state leaders at Iowa's Purple Star Schools launch
items.hook: Seventeen schools became Iowa's first Purple Star Schools, building stronger support for military-connected students.
items.quote: When schools understand military life, students are better positioned to thrive through moves, deployment, and transition.
body: Iowa officially launched its Purple Star School Program during Month of the Military Child, marking a major milestone in statewide support for military-connected students.

The program grew from years of collaboration across education and military communities. Senate File 275 created the foundation, and Iowa became the 44th state to adopt the nationally recognized designation.
Purple Star Schools establish visible resources, trained staff, and practical systems that help students navigate frequent moves, disrupted learning, and separation from a parent.
items.impact: Seven districts representing 17 schools earned Iowa's first designations and demonstrated that consistent school support is part of family readiness.

gallery.alt: Iowa's first Purple Star School recognition ceremony

items.title: Purple Up! Day Reaches Classrooms Across Iowa
items.alt: Purple Up Day classroom kit outreach across Iowa
items.hook: Ready-to-use classroom kits helped thousands of Iowa students recognize and celebrate military children.
items.quote: Recognition gives military-connected students a moment of pride instead of invisibility.
body: Classrooms across Iowa marked Purple Up! Day with educational kits designed to explain military life and celebrate the resilience of military children.
The materials made participation easy for educators while giving students shared language for moves, deployment, and the experiences of military families.
By bringing Month of the Military Child into classrooms, Iowa CYP extended support into the place where day-to-day belonging matters most.
items.impact: More than 130 kits reached 68 schools and approximately 3,850 youth, including many families connecting with Iowa CYP for the first time.

gallery.alt: Purple Up Day classroom outreach materials

items.title: Iowa Recognizes Month of the Military Child
items.alt: Governor Reynolds signing the Month of the Military Child proclamation at the Iowa Capitol
items.hook: Military families and youth stood together as April was officially proclaimed Month of the Military Child.
items.quote: Public recognition tells military children that their resilience, service, and sacrifice are seen.
body: Military-connected youth and families gathered at the Iowa Capitol as Governor Reynolds officially proclaimed April as Month of the Military Child across the state.
The proclamation launched a month of classroom outreach, visibility efforts, and community celebrations coordinated with schools and partners.
Standing together in the Capitol made military children's experiences visible and connected family stories to Iowa's broader readiness mission.
items.impact: More than 35 family members, including State Teen Panel youth, helped open a statewide month of recognition and support.

gallery.alt: Month of the Military Child proclamation ceremony

items.title: Moments That Stay With Us
items.alt: State Teen Panel members visiting veterans in Boone, Iowa
items.hook: Teen leaders sat with veterans to hear personal stories of service, sacrifice, and life after the uniform.
items.quote: The experience you gain and the time spent away from family made service feel personal instead of distant.
body: State Teen Panel members spent the day at Eastern Star Masonic Home in Boone listening to veterans share stories of service, sacrifice, and life after the uniform.
For the teens, the visit offered context for family separation, resilience, and the long view of what military life can ask of a person.
What began as a service project became a bridge between generations and a reminder that listening is itself a form of leadership.
items.impact: The visit strengthened empathy and service-minded leadership while honoring veterans whose experiences continue to teach the next generation.

gallery.alt: State Teen Panel members during their veteran community visit

items.title: Iowa Teen Steps Into Statewide Leadership
items.alt: Charlee Cromwell volunteering at a food packaging line
items.hook: Charlee Cromwell was selected to help carry Iowa youth perspectives into Guard Teen Panel conversations.
items.quote: That experience helped me realize I wanted to use my voice to support other military teens across our region.
body: For many military teens, leadership begins quietly by showing up, listening, and choosing to serve. For Charlee, that steady commitment led to a statewide role.
As Iowa's Guard Teen Panel representative, she brings youth perspectives into planning, outreach, and leadership conversations that shape military youth programs.
Her path reflects the strength of Iowa CYP's leadership pipeline, where responsibility and trust are earned through consistent service.
items.impact: Peer leadership gives military-connected teens an active role in shaping programs built around their real experiences.

items.title: Fall Family Festival Strengthens Guard Connections
items.alt: Guard families gathered at Camp Dodge Fall Family Festival
items.hook: Camp Dodge became a reunion space filled with activities, partners, and Guard family connection.
items.quote: Community-backed events help Guard families feel seen, supported, and less alone.
body: Military families gathered at Camp Dodge for a day built around connection, resilience, and readiness. The installation felt like a reunion space for Guard-connected kids, parents, and caregivers.
State Teen Panel members, community partners, therapy-animal volunteers, and activity leaders created shared experiences that helped families relax and reconnect.
Events like this reduce isolation, strengthen peer connection, and remind families that they belong to something larger than a single event day.
items.impact: Nearly half of participating families were new to Iowa CYP, expanding the network of support available across the Guard community.

gallery.alt: Families enjoying the Fall Family Festival at Camp Dodge

items.title: Chain of Confidence: A Camper's Turnaround
items.alt: Joseph smiling with mentor Chris inside the rec hall
items.hook: A small challenge and a patient mentor turned homesickness into pride by the middle of camp week.
items.quote: He started the week wanting to go home. By Wednesday, he was leading with confidence.
body: On Monday, one camper sat off to the side fighting back tears and asking to go home. The first day of camp can feel uncertain and overwhelming.
A small challenge, patient encouragement, and one hard-earned win changed the week. By Wednesday, the same camper was standing tall, smiling, and connected.
Camp gives youth room to struggle, support to keep going, and confidence built through a real success they can carry home.
items.impact: Sometimes a child needs one achievable challenge and one adult who believes they can do it. Consistent mentorship can turn a difficult beginning into a lasting breakthrough.

gallery.alt: Joseph celebrating his camp breakthrough with mentor Chris

items.title: Legacy Rock Friendship
items.alt: Isla and Rylee holding a painted rock together and laughing
items.hook: Two campers arrived as strangers and left with a friendship built to continue through moves and transitions.
items.quote: Some of the strongest bonds begin when military-connected kids realize someone else understands.
body: At first glance, it is a picture of two smiling girls and a painted rock. Behind the smiles is a friendship that formed quickly at summer camp.
Rylee and Isla arrived as strangers and became inseparable. Their legacy rock made the week visible and lasting, capturing what connection can look like when kids feel safe and understood.
Even with a move ahead, they left camp planning how to stay in touch. Their friendship outlasted the event that introduced them.
items.impact: Shared camp experiences give military-connected youth relationships that can remain steady through relocation, deployment, and change.

gallery.alt: Isla and Rylee with the legacy rock that represents their friendship

items.title: Altoona Teen Honored for Service to Guard Families
items.alt: Klaryssa Klair Dunwoody volunteering with the State Teen Panel
items.hook: Klair's service with the State Teen Panel earned statewide recognition and strengthened support for younger Guard youth.
items.quote: Service became her way of shaping the Guard family experience for other kids.
body: Military childhood can bring challenges that are easy for others to miss. For Klaryssa Klair Dunwoody, those challenges became an invitation to lead.
Through the State Teen Panel, Klair helped plan and support family events while becoming a reliable presence for younger youth and parents navigating Guard life.
Her dedication earned the 2023 Iowa Army National Guard Youth Volunteer Award and showed other teens that youth leadership is part of the mission.
items.impact: When military-connected teens step forward to serve, they strengthen the Guard family community from the inside out.

gallery.alt: Klair serving through the Iowa State Teen Panel
